identity.title: OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic bulge: I. Colour, CO line, and stellar light curve characteristics

paper_type_evidence.quote: Observations of circumstellar lines from several rotational transitions of $^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, and C$^{18}$O were performed with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), and, for a sub-sample, with the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment telescope (APEX).

The sample of 77 OH/IR stars was observed with ALMA band 3 (cite: clauetal08), 6 (cite: edisetal04), and 7 (cite: mahietal12) receivers to cover the $^{12}$CO $J$ = 1–0, 2–1, and 3–2, and the $^{13}$CO $J$ = 2–1 and 3–2 lines (project 2023.1.00098.S).

question.value: Obtain information on the mass loss of O-rich AGB stars, and on its transformations in geometry and kinematics that occur at the tip of the AGB.

evidence.quote: We used an equidistant sample of 77 AGB stars in the inner Galactic bulge, selected on the existence and strength of OH1612 MHz maser emission, to obtain information on the mass loss of O-rich AGB stars, and on its transformations in geometry and kinematics that occur at the tip of the AGB.

analysis_steps.goal: Characterize infrared SEDs, variability, and classify objects into four categories

method.value: Correct Spitzer, MSX, and WISE photometry for extinction; construct mid-IR colour-colour diagrams to separate standard (SdE) and detached (DdE) dust envelopes; fit single-period sinusoids to VVV Ks and WISE W1/W2 light curves to separate regular large-amplitude pulsators (P) from non-periodic/low-amplitude (nP); inspect 12CO moment 8 maps and line profiles to separate standard (SgE) and complex (CgE) gas envelopes.

evidence.quote: Based on these data, we constructed two colour-colour diagrams: $S_{7.87}/S_{4.49}$ vs $S_{22.1}/S_{7.87}$ and $S_{14.65}/S_{8.28}$ vs $S_{21.34}/S_{14.65}$.
We used maximum intensity $^{12}$CO images (moment 8 in CASA), over the circumstellar velocity ranges, to characterize their morphologies.

We regard an object as a large-amplitude, regular pulsator (P) if the period is well-determined and the amplitude is $>$ 0.5 mag, with an uncertainty lower than 20 % of its value, in at least one band.
These borders are mathematically described by the expressions $S_{22.1}/S_{7.87}$ = 30$\times$($S_{7.87}/S_{4.49})^{-0.8}$ and $S_{21.34}/S_{14.65}$ = 40 $\times$ ($S_{14.65}/S_{8.28})^{-3}$.

claims.hypothesis: High-mass-loss O-rich AGB and post-AGB (OH/IR) stars in the inner Galactic bulge can be systematically classified as they evolve up and off the tip of the AGB using infrared SED, CO line, and variability properties.
claims.experiment: Constructed mid-IR colour-colour diagrams (Spitzer, MSX, WISE), analysed VVV Ks and WISE W1/W2 light curves, and mapped 12CO and 13CO rotational lines with ALMA for 77 inner Galactic bulge OH/IR stars.
claims.result: The 74 CO-detected stars cleanly divide into bimodal distributions (SdE vs DdE, SgE vs CgE, P vs nP) forming four categories: SSP (40), SSnP (7), DSnP (10), and DCnP (17), with all 40 regular pulsators having standard attached dust and spherical gas envelopes (SSP) and all 17 complex gas envelopes having detached dust envelopes and non-periodic light curves (DCnP).
claims.finding: OH/IR stars separate into four evolutionary/morphological categories with distinct C18O(2-1) and 338 GHz continuum detection rates.

evidence.quote: Remarkably, as will be shown below, for each of these characteristics our objects clearly divide, with only a few exceptions, into two types: attached (‘standard’) versus detached dust-CSEs, standard versus complex gas-CSEs, and periodic versus non-periodic light curves.
There are 40 objects in category SdE/SgE/P (SSP), seven objects in category SdE/SgE/nP (SSnP), ten objects in category DdE/SgE/nP (DSnP), and 17 objects in category DdE/CgE/nP (DCnP).

claims.hypothesis: Standard gas-CSE (SgE) OH/IR stars share homogeneous large-scale circumstellar gas properties where higher-J and rarer isotopologue CO transitions trace progressively more compact, optically thicker inner regions.
claims.experiment: Fitted Moffat profiles to azimuthally averaged radial brightness profiles (AARPs) and 'Shell' profiles to multi-aperture (0.5'' to 3'') ALMA spectra of 12CO(1-0, 2-1, 3-2) and 13CO(2-1, 3-2) for 57 SgE objects.
claims.result: Average Theta_0.1 decreases from 1.01'' in 12CO(1-0) to 0.57'' in 12CO(2-1) and 0.36'' in 12CO(3-2) (and 0.46'' to 0.29'' in 13CO 2-1 to 3-2), while line shapes evolve from flat-topped (H = -0.22 for 12CO 1-0) to parabolic (H = -0.73 for 12CO 3-2) with low 12CO/13CO intensity ratios (average 3.4 +- 1.2).
claims.finding: SgE OH/IR stars have highly homogeneous large-scale gas-CSEs whose transition sizes and line shapes follow optical depth and excitation expectations, and suggest low circumstellar 12CO/13CO abundance ratios.

evidence.loc: Azimuthally averaged CO line radial brightness profiles
evidence.quote: On average, for the $^{12}$CO lines, the extent of the 1$-$0 emission is $\approx$ 80 % larger than that of the 2$-$1 emission, which in turn is $\approx$ 60 % larger than the 3$-$2 emission.

evidence.loc: Line intensity ratios: Different transitions and isotopologues
evidence.quote: We calculated the $^{12}$CO/$^{13}$CO line intensity ratios for the 2$-$1 and 3$-$2 lines in the same way as above. They are surprisingly low, 1.5$-$8 with an average of 3.4 $\pm$ 1.2 (the two lines combined).

Thus, it is expected that the $^{12}$CO lines stretch from close to rectangular ($H$ = $-$0.22, the 1$-$0 line) to close to parabolic ($H$ = $-$0.73, the 3$-$2 line), and the $^{13}$CO lines are more flat-topped than the corresponding $^{12}$CO lines.

claims.hypothesis: Millimetre continuum emission detected by ALMA from these inner Galactic bulge OH/IR stars arises from circumstellar dust rather than the stellar photosphere.
claims.experiment: Measured continuum flux densities at 107, 233, and 338 GHz via 2D Gaussian fitting and derived spectral indices across bands, comparing with a 2500 K, 5500 L_sun blackbody at 8.2 kpc.
claims.result: Detected 3, 18, and 33 objects at 107, 233, and 338 GHz with steep average spectral indices of 3.5 +- 0.6 (SgE) and 3.3 +- 0.3 (CgE), whereas a stellar blackbody yields ~0.04 mJy at 338 GHz (well below the 0.2 mJy/beam rms).
claims.finding: Detected ALMA continuum emission is dominated by circumstellar dust emission (with one flat-spectrum exception, OH002.640-0.191).

evidence.quote: When detections are made in more than one band, the flux densities result in an average spectral index $\alpha$ ($S_\nu$ $\propto$ $\nu^\alpha$) of 3.5 $\pm$ 0.6 (ten objects). The continuum flux at 338 GHz of a 2500 K blackbody of luminosity 5500 $L_\odot$ (typical for our sources) at the distance of the Galactic centre is about 0.04 mJy. This is well below our detection limit, and it, combined with the spectral index estimates, implies that any detected continuum emission from AGB stars at that distance is due to circumstellar dust emission.

claims.hypothesis: Interferometric filtering by ALMA in the 3'' aperture data does not cause severe flux loss for the circumstellar CO(2-1) and CO(3-2) lines.
claims.experiment: Observed a sub-sample of 23 high-velocity, off-plane stars with the APEX 12 m single-dish telescope in 12CO and 13CO (2-1 and 3-2) and compared velocity-integrated intensities with ALMA 3'' aperture values after removing CSM/ISM-contaminated sources.
claims.result: Average ALMA(3'')/APEX intensity ratios are 0.87 +- 0.22 for 12CO(2-1), 0.72 +- 0.24 for 12CO(3-2), 0.95 +- 0.38 for 13CO(2-1), and 0.87 +- 0.31 for 13CO(3-2).
claims.finding: Typical interferometric flux loss in the ALMA 3'' CO line data is at the <= 20% level.

evidence.quote: Taking everything into consideration, the results indicate that the typical flux loss in the ALMA data is at the $\ensuremath{\lesssim}$ 20 % level.

why_this_data.value: Selecting OH/IR stars in the inner Galactic bulge with OH 1612 MHz flux > 0.3 Jy and luminosity within a factor of two of 5400 L_sun provides an equidistant (~8.2 kpc), statistically significant sample of 77 high-mass-loss O-rich AGB stars in a narrow initial-mass range, overcoming the small sample size (15 stars) and limited S/N and transition coverage of O+22.

evidence.quote: The study of O+22 had limitations. Only two $^{12}$CO lines and one $^{13}$CO line were observed, often with limited S/N. The limited sample size (15 objects) prevented statistical comparisons. In the present study we remedy these shortcomings by observing 77 objects in the inner Galactic bulge in different CO isotopologue lines with ALMA and a sub-sample with the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment telescope (APEX).

We selected all objects, brighter than 0.3 Jy in the OH 1612 MHz line, that have an estimated luminosity within a factor of two of the median luminosity of the O+22 sample, 5400 $L_\odot$. This minimized contamination by foreground objects, and helped ensure that the sample covers a narrow range in initial mass.

why_this_method.value: Convolving cubes to 0.5'', 1'', 2'', and 3'' circular Gaussian beams and extracting central-pixel spectra balances S/N degradation at larger apertures (due to non-white interferometer noise) against capturing extended emission, while Moffat profile fits to azimuthally averaged radial profiles boost S/N on weak extended emission.

evidence.loc: Azimuthally averaged CO line radial brightness profiles
evidence.quote: In order to study them in more detail we derived azimuthally averaged radial brightness profiles (AARPs) by azimuthally averaging the data cubes for all objects and for all lines within the velocity range $\pm$20 % of the gas expansion velocity centred on the systemic velocity. This increases the S/N and provides more reliable information on the weak, extended emission.

The CO line brightness distributions are sharply peaked for SgE objects, but they contain extended low-intensity emission as shown above. This, together with the limited S/N of the data and the fact that the S/N decreases for a compact source when using increasingly larger apertures (cite: tsuketal23), makes it difficult to estimate the total intensities of the interferometer data. We therefore summarise the observational $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO line results in a way suitable for the radiative transfer analysis of SgE objects.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Excluding short baselines (spatial scales > 3-5'') to filter out interstellar CO contamination was tested on uncontaminated strong sources and rejected (except for two objects: OH359.161-0.055 and OH000.319-0.041) because it caused significant loss of circumstellar flux.

evidence.quote: Because the lines of sight to the Galactic centre are crowded with interstellar CO line emission, the imaging was done twice for the CO lines, first with full range of visibilities and then excluding short baselines corresponding to spatial frequencies lower than 3–5 $''$, in order to exploit the filtering capabilities of the interferometer and limit the line-of-sight contamination from interstellar CO line emission. The latter approach was tested on a number of objects with strong circumstellar lines and no interstellar contamination and showed significant amounts of lost circumstellar flux in all cases. Hence, except for two objects, we refrained from using short-baseline removal as a solution to this problem.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using the Moffat SWHM (Theta_0.5) or surface integral of the Moffat fit to measure source size and total flux was rejected because Theta_0.5 is close to the synthesised beam FWHM and average beta values are < 2 (so the integral does not converge at reasonable radii); Theta_0.1 was used instead.

evidence.loc: Azimuthally averaged CO line radial brightness profiles
evidence.quote: The $\Theta_{0.5}$ values are, on average, close to the FWHMs of the synthesised beams, and not a good measure of the extent of the brightness distribution (cite: ramsetal20).

evidence.loc: Azimuthally averaged CO line radial brightness profiles
evidence.quote: The average $\beta$:s are all below 2, and we cannot use these fits to reliably estimate the total flux densities. We instead chose the angular extent at which the fit to the AARP reaches 10 % of its peak value, $\Theta_{0.1}$, as a measure of the size of the brightness distribution

limitations_admitted.value: Lines of sight toward the Galactic centre suffer from interstellar CO line emission (~10% of objects) and extended CSM/ISM interaction emission (~20% of objects), complicating line profile extraction and ALMA-APEX comparisons.

evidence.quote: About 20 % of the objects show extended structures, often with low surface brightness, that can possibly be attributed to interaction between circumstellar and interstellar CO gas (CSM/ISM). Another about 10 % of the objects show clear presence of interstellar CO line emission in the velocity range of the circumstellar emission.

limitations_admitted.value: Part of the 13CO(3-2) line fell outside the spectral window for seven objects despite splitting Band 7 into two velocity tunings.

evidence.quote: Despite this, part of the $^{13}$CO(3–2) line was missed for seven objects (for three of these objects the data of O+22 were used instead).

limitations_admitted.value: Some spread in source distances along the line of sight around the adopted 8.2 kpc is likely, and none of the sources have reliable Gaia EDR3 parallaxes.

evidence.quote: The adopted distance to all of our sources is 8.2 kpc (cite: gravcoll19), even though some spread along the line of sight is most likely. Unfortunately, none of our sources have a measured reliable parallax in Gaia Early Data Release 3 (cite: gaiacoll23).

limitations_admitted.value: Extended low-surface-brightness dust continuum emission at large radii (> 1.9'' MRS at 338 GHz) may be resolved out by the interferometer or missed by 2D Gaussian fits.

evidence.quote: It is likely that there is continuum flux not captured by the fitted Gaussians nor ‘seen’ by the interferometer. Extended low-surface brightness emission from colder dust at large radii may contribute (maybe even significantly) to the flux measured by ALMA.

limitations_admitted.value: For CgE objects with high-velocity wings, limited S/N means reported FWZPs (50 to 150 km s^-1) are likely lower limits, and some bipolar outflows may be misclassified as SgE due to orientation or weak wings.

evidence.quote: There may be objects with higher-velocity wings that are too weak to be detected or the orientation is such that the wings are not seen if the outflow is bipolar, i.e. there may be border line objects between SgE and CgE.

For CgE objects with line wings, the FWZPs range from about 50 to 150  km s$^{-1}$. The S/N of our spectra are in general limited, so the reported values are likely to be lower limits to the true FWZPs.

referee_caveats_inferred: Classification between SgE and CgE relies partly on visual inspection of moment 8 images and line profiles, which can be sensitive to S/N and viewing inclination.
No radiative transfer modelling is performed in this paper; physical mass-loss rates and 12C/13C abundance ratios are deferred to forthcoming papers.
